title: Critique my answer: 'How would you evaluate a RAG system?'
body:
> **Casebook thread.** A reconstructed conversation, written for teaching. The people in it
> are illustrative; **every number is real** and reproducible from the notebook cited below.
> Replies are welcome — if you hit this yourself, add your numbers.

Practising the most commonly asked question in this space. Here is my answer — please tear it
apart.

---

**My answer:**

> "I'd build an eval set with questions and expected answers, then measure accuracy. I'd also track
> retrieval metrics like recall and precision, and use an LLM to judge answer quality since exact
> match is too strict. I'd run it in CI so we catch regressions."

---

### Self-critique before anyone else does

It is **correct, generic, and could have been written by someone who has never run one.**

- "questions and expected answers" — no **gold evidence**, so I cannot separate a retrieval failure
  from a generation one, or detect a right-by-accident
- "measure accuracy" — against what baseline? I have not said what the number means
- "an LLM to judge" — no calibration, no κ, no base rate. I have added an unmeasured instrument
- "run it in CI" — on what threshold? A gate with no noise band blocks correct changes
- **no interval anywhere**, which is the thing this whole repository is about

comments.body:
> **Dana** · reviewer · owns the eval harness

The self-critique is stronger than the answer, which is the right way round.

One thing you have not caught: **"expected answers" quietly assumes the answers exist.** On a real
engagement they do not, and the first two weeks are manufacturing them. A panel asking this is
often really asking *"have you ever built an eval set from nothing?"* — and the answer that scores
says so before being asked.

replies.body:
> **Priya** · cohort peer

Also: **"retrieval metrics" plural is doing a lot of hiding.** "Recall and precision" collapses at
least three measurements over two different denominators. Say it in a round and you will be asked
which — and the answer had better not be improvised.

comments.body:
Marking this, because the shape matters as much as the content.

---

**A stronger answer, roughly as I would say it out loud:**

> "It depends on whether they have labels, and usually they do not — so I'd start with the first
> two weeks rather than describing a finished harness.
>
> **The eval set is the work.** I need questions, and for each one the **gold evidence**, not just
> the expected answer. Without evidence labels I cannot tell a retrieval failure from a generation
> failure, and I cannot detect the case that matters most: the answer is right and nothing relevant
> was retrieved. That means the model knew it already and retrieval is decorative for that query.
>
> I'd include **null questions at their real base rate**, because without them I cannot measure
> abstention at all, and a system that never refuses looks perfect on a set with nothing
> unanswerable in it.
>
> Then measure at each stage separately: did the evidence reach the pool, did it survive into the
> prompt, did the model use it. Three booleans, four verdicts, and the **distribution** over fifty
> failures decides where the month goes.
>
> Before any of that means anything I need two baselines: the **noise band**, bootstrapped on the
> unchanged system, and the **ungrounded floor** — what the model scores with no retrieved context
> at all.
>
> On the judge: I would not use one until I had calibrated it against a couple of hundred hand
> labels and could report Cohen's κ **with the base rate beside it**. 94% agreement on a 90/10 split
> is κ around 0.6; on 95/5 the same 94% is κ 0.37.
>
> In CI the gate blocks on a pre-registered primary metric regressing beyond the noise band, and on
> any slice regressing beyond **its own** band — a slice of 30 has a much wider interval than the
> full set, and gating it with the aggregate band fails constantly on noise until somebody disables
> the gate."

---

## Why this scores

1. **It leads with the constraint** — no labels — rather than a finished system. The shape of the
   answer reveals whether you have done this before the content does.
2. **It names the failure mode nobody names**: right by accident, and the ungrounded floor that
   detects it.
3. **It has numbers in it.** κ 0.6 versus 0.37 on the same 94% cannot be improvised, and one
   concrete number does more work than three correct paragraphs.
4. **It knows what a gate costs.** "A gate that blocks correct changes gets disabled" is the
   sentence that says you have operated one.

## What would still not survive a hard follow-up

You have not said **how many questions**. The honest answer is that it depends on the effect size
you need to detect, and the arithmetic is
[here](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/blob/main/docs/30-learning/interview-prep/01-mathematical-foundations/paired-bootstrap-and-power.md).
Have it ready — it is the most common second question.
